The house resumed, from Monday, March 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Garson

Economic Position of Agriculture (for Mr. Harris) for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

Last evening before the adjournment my remarks were being directed toward that phase of the agricultural industry which in my province plays a generally recognized part, that which is classified as mixed farming. I assure you it was not the growing and prosperous picture I should like to have been able to disclose in connection with this great national asset.
However, in the agricultural industry, as in others, there are exceptions, and there are various degrees of prosperity. Generally speaking one finds a higher degree of prosperity in areas where dairying is more or less the dominant phase of agriculture. There is some stability to it. It has received assistance by way of protection and floor prices and, with the growing consumption of milk and related products, it is a far more stable part of the agricultural industry than some others. In the dairy areas in my province one finds far more steady prosperity.
I understand that approximately one-sixth of the population of our country depends upon this industry. Therefore it needs protection. It needs not only the protection it has; it needs more protection to keep it such a great industry, and it needs assistance to keep it stable. In my opinion that comes within the purview of this resolution.
Another exception I should like to mention, in so far as my own constituency is concerned, is an industry in which I am vitally interested, the potato industry. We have the small grower who mixes this crop with other crops, and we have the large producer who has specialized in the potato industry to the exclusion of all other crops. Some of our most prosperous farmers are those who have specialized in potato production. Within my constituency can be seen some of the finest rural homes that can be found anywhere in the province. These producers have lovely buildings, good farms, between 200 and 500 acres, and plenty of equipment, and they enjoy a degree of prosperity much higher than the great mass of farmers.
Unfortunately we do not have enough of this type of farmers, and the areas are small where this prosperity seems to accumulate. Over the years a percentage of our large potato growers have been fortunate and have prospered in this most difficult and uncertain phase of agriculture. However, whilst this


group is small percentage-wise, it is a very important group nevertheless and contributes greatly to our local economic situation and the outlook in general in connection with our national economy. But during the past few years it has been caught in the cost-price squeeze, just as other farmers have. These producers have had only one good year in the last five, and much of this accumulated wealth-these beautiful homes that you see and the large amount of equipment-is commencing to dwindle. Many of those people who have prospered are commencing to find that their wealth is dwindling, and some of them are having a difficult time to get cash with which to pay their bills. This is a most unfortunate situation in a part of agriculture that should be more stable.
I should like to give an illustration. It is a general illustration but I think it will bring out the point that was impressed upon the hon. members of this house yesterday. I hold in my hand the potato report which I get daily. It is dated yesterday, March 12. I will take as an example this city of Ottawa. Wholesalers were paying for potatoes in this city yesterday an average of 2i cents a pound. In order to make a fairly close check I contacted some of my farmers at home. I find that the price they were getting last Friday, Saturday and yesterday permits the farmer to clear over his cost of production- out of that 2J cents a pound-between one-fifth and one-quarter of a cent. If you want to put it into bushels, it will give him between 15 and 20 cents a bushel. Out of that 15 to 20 cents a bushel for growing his potatoes he has to live, pay his taxes and provide for the interest on the capital which he has invested.
I think that example clearly demonstrates the extremely narrow margin on which our farmers are working. That is the highest price that has been paid for potatoes this season-and the season begins about the middle of September or the first of September-with the exception of a few local lots which are of the very early variety. Two and a half cents a pound may seem to be quite a good price. By the time the consumer gets the potatoes I have no doubt it is about cents a pound. But what we are trying to impress upon the government is what the farmer gets for his labour in producing his crop. I think that example demonstrates the situation clearly. Whether you take the farmers on an average or whether you take them individually, the net amount they receive is very small.
It seems to me that the situation illustrates another point which I suppose I should mention to the Minister of Agriculture before

sitting down. I think it demonstrates clearly to him why the potato growers did not joyfully and thankfully receive that starch diversion program which this government offered them in January. I suppose the way they look at it is that they might as well lose money in one way as in another. However, at $1 a barrel they just cannot break even. When potatoes are priced from $2 to $2.15, as they are today and were yesterday and Friday, they can make merely a little profit. We need more stability. There are those people who take a chance and in some years they make a great deal of money; in other years they lose a great deal of money. That is not good for agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to fairly sum up the agricultural situation, in my province and generally. I believe that the average is much the same all over eastern Canada. The west, where there are large wheat growers, I know nothing about. However, I think the progress of the farmer is fairly clearly demonstrated. We will put it this way. It is lagging far behind the progress of other groups in this country, and I do not think that is a sound situation.
I am going to quote a few words here as follows:
The way of life of the farmer is itself a great national asset and his prosperity is the foundation of national prosperity.
I wonder whether any of the hon. members opposite have ever heard those words before? In case they have forgotten I will tell them that they were part of the national federal Liberal program in 1948. The statement continued:
It is the policy of the Liberal party to foster that prosperity through secure markets at fair prices.
I am quite ready to leave it to the farmers of this country to judge whether or not this government has carried out this pledge to agriculture. It is not for me to be the judge. I think the principle is sound and I can agree with it. I think this government should make every effort to carry it out, or there should be some explanation as to why they cannot do so.
I believe the farmers are entitled to a fair price for what they produce and sell in relation to prices they have to pay for the goods they must purchase. Surely they are entitled to a fair return on their capital investment. Surely they should not be expected to work double the hours worked by other groups and get less and, as a matter of fact, sometimes not break even.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I believe in the principle enunciated in
Economic Position of Agriculture this amendment. I believe it can be implemented successfully, and I support it. I again affirm my opinion that the farmers of this country are entitled to nothing less.

Mr. Speaker, I had thought
that the matters which have been discussed yesterday and again today might have been discussed on my estimates. I had therefore intended to make at that time any remarks which I am going to make now. In view of what has been said and the fact that the question is in the minds of most hon. members at the moment, I think probably I should deal now with the remarks which have been made.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in bringing forward his amendment to the motion to go into supply, moved it in these words:

Hear, hear.

I will say "hear, hear" to that also. The only policy the government of Canada has in connection with the marketing of wheat is the wheat board. The

wheat board was set up by this government in its present form as a compulsory marketing board to handle the wheat of the farmer through a board to which the farmers are compelled to deliver their wheat. It was set up under this government in 1943. I know that my friends on the other side of the house like to say it was first advocated -in this house, I presume; it was advocated outside of it earlier than that-by the late Mr. Bennett, and it was. But again I repeat that when Mr. Bennett brought it into the house he had the biggest majority there ever was in this house prior to that time, and he was not able to put it through. He therefore withdrew it.
He was forced to.
I hear some of my friends saying he was forced to yield. But I should like to see my friends opposite force us to do some particular thing under similar circumstances.
We did last year.

As a matter of fact there were so many men sitting on the government side of the house at that time who did not believe in that policy that Mr. Bennett was not able to put it through, and he made apologies for his own party later on. Nevertheless the legislation was put through in a particular form, and later on we found it advisable to make it a compulsory board.
That has been the policy of this government ever since. We have taken over the marketing of wheat by a wheat board which the farmers wanted. We have said to them, "Go ahead and market that wheat" and we have given them all the facilities and powers necessary to make it possible for them to market it. Again the Canadian Federation of Agriculture says that policy is the right policy and they are in agreement with it. It also urges that every effort be made to bring about a satisfactory renewal of the international wheat agreement. The minister concerned has reported on that matter to the house from time to time, and has indicated that everything possible is being done to bring about that result, although we are not in a position to state whether it will be successful.
Finally, on behalf again of our prairie grain producers, we would endorse the quota system of grain marketing,-
Again that was introduced by this government, through the wheat board of course, but before the wheat board had the power it has at the present time.
-with the request that this system be continued, and combined with a distribution of box cars as between shipping points that will make space available on an equitable basis.
Econoviic Position of Agriculture
Then they come down to feed freight assistance:
We would simply repeat our request that this policy be continued, and further ask that it be given full recognition as a permanent national policy by being embodied in special legislation rather than maintained by order in council.
That is another policy of this government which they support. They did not come here asking for something different on all these matters. They came here to encourage us to go on to do more, because we had been doing the things which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture thought ought to be done. They go on to deal with international trade arrangements, emphasizing the point they made with regard to dairy products. Then third they recognize the wisdom of individual countries, including our own, so managing their domestic affairs as to keep to a minimum the necessity of imposing import restrictions or selling export surpluses at less than domestic prices.
Then they go on to support the government marketing some of this butter-the small amount they have in addition to what is needed here-outside of this country. Then they deal with farm credits, and they say this:
This second statement of policy which we are presenting for your consideration at this time deals with the subject of farm credit. This statement has already been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance because of the fact that the legislation dealing with the Canadian farm loan board has been opened up and was due for early consideration by parliament.
That is another thing they agree with. Then they go on to say this:
There are a number of very specific recommenda-tains contained in this farm credit policy,-
That was put out in a separate document.
-and we will at this time mention only the major features. In general they are aimed at reducing the cost, and broadening and liberalizing the various provisions of our federal farm credit institutions.
Of course they go on to say they would like to have a lower interest. They think maybe the interest rate ought to be per cent, and they make strong representations to that effect. But the principle of the legislation which has been introduced into this house in order to provide credit for farmers, farm improvement loans and farm loans, which was in effect before this present government came into power, and which has been changed somewhat since-they are in favour of all those policies and simply say they would like to have a lower rate of interest upon them, if that is possible.
To establish a policy for providing emergency or disaster credit on an interest-free basis where the nature and extent of a farmer's loss justifies the granting of such credit.

Economic Position of Agriculture
That was their final request, and they went on to refer to something that was taking place in the province of British Columbia, where strawberry plants had been frozen and where other difficulties had arisen. Again it has been pointed out to British Columbia and to others that legislation of that kind should originate in the provinces. The federal government has not said what assistance it would give if such legislation were passed. They have left it in the hands of the provincial governments to determine whether they are going to do anything and what they are going to do in order to meet the situation before the federal government says anything with regard to it.
That is the presentation in so far as agriculture is concerned. They have dealt with other matters such as radio, television and so on, but I am not going into those matters. What I wish to say to the hon. member for Prince Albert is this. If he thinks, as he did back in 1941, that this government ought to follow the policies which are supported by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture; if he will go back and read those policies now and check up on what has been done by the federal government since then, if he will then read this presentation he will find in it only commendation for the government for what they have done. There is no criticism of the policies that have been put into effect but only commendation for what they have done, and then suggesting a few ways in which it might be possible to improve upon the action taken.
If my hon. friends do not find that strong enough, and if they think that Mr. Hannam was speaking to the government and therefore might not have said that to his own organization, I read you just this from his speech to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
Our present butter program is a case in point.
This is after having indicated the things that have been done.
It is difficult to conceive of a farm program that is more considerate of consumers and taxpayers interests than this one.
It maintains a ceiling for consumers at about 64 or 65 cents retail, when without it the price of butter might easily go to 80 or 90 cents in winter months as it did several years ago when the board held no stocks. It has not lowered quality. It has cost, on the average, less than $1 million a year-
That was indicated by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton) yesterday.
-yet spokesmen for consumers and taxpayers are advocating an alternative type of support program designed to lower the price to the consumer while still maintaining 58 cent support for the producer. They have not explained that, if that type of


program were adopted and it succeeded in a substantial lowering of the retail price of butter, it would probably cost the treasury up to $10 to $20 million each year.
In other words, he is supporting the government policy there.
Would the minister allow a question?
Yes.
Did the minister write Mr. Hannam's speech?

Well, that is just another way of saying, Mr. Speaker, that the president of the federation of agriculture is in such close agreement with the policies of this government that my hon. friend thinks I must have written his speech. Of course, Mr. Hannam comes from the same part of the country as my hon. friend, and he knows that nobody up in that part of the country, not even the hon. member, would allow anyone to write his speech for him.
The suggestion has been made that we should have parity prices. It has been suggested that the federation agrees that we ought to have parity prices. I have in my hand what the federation has agreed to, and what they have said we ought to do. They were in favour of having a mathematical formula worked out which they thought everyone might be able to understand and from which we would arrive at support prices for our different products. In order to explain what they had in mind, they said this:
Calculation of modernized basic prices (calculated according to the formula recommended by the C.F.A. national farm policy committee.)
It was passed eventually by the federation itself meeting in Edmonton last year. They illustrate here the way it works. The average price of No. 1 wheat, Fort William, 1943-44 to 1952-53, $1.75; index of wholesale prices of farm products 1944-53, 150-9. Then, 1925-29 being taken as 100, cost of commodities and services including living costs, western provinces, in 1953 equals 176-3; then the basic price for wheat, 1954-55 equals $1.75 multiplied by 100 over 150-9 times 176-3 over 100 equals $1.16 multiplied by 176-3 over 100 or $2.05 a bushel, and that is parity. They say the range that should be acknowledged in setting support prices should be from 65 to 85 per cent of the basic price, which would be from $1.33 to $1.74 per bushel, basis Fort William. The floor price which is set, and has been set for years, is $1.40, which is between those two prices of $1.33 and $1.74.
Well, they worked out another one here, and I am not going all through it as I did the first one. It is for good steers. When they finish the calculation they say that parity

price should be $23.06. I think that is very close to the price that was worked out by the farmers' union when they were here a week or two ago. Some hon. members were quoting from the farm union brief. Unfortunately for the farmers' union, as compared with the federation, the farmers' union says that floor prices ought to be parity prices. In connection with the $23.06 the federation says the range of floor prices ought to be anywhere from 65 to 85 per cent of the basic price, or between $14.99 and $19.60 per hundred. When I first read this document, that is exactly what beef cattle were, $19.60, the highest price at which they said there should be a floor. It has been up a little and it has been down a little since, but generally speaking that floor is satisfactory to them.
I have a list here of the calculations for the different products we were talking about. I have already covered wheat and I have covered steers. Eighty-five per cent of the steer price at Toronto is $19.60. That is not the price at the moment, but that is the price stated here as being the top floor price. As a matter of fact, when the federation concluded with this they said they did not want floor prices on cattle. The floor price is worked out here on this sheet, but they say in the statement that they do not want floor prices on cattle.
Why do they say that? They say that because they agree with the government that the floor price we have now is the highest price you can obtain anywhere in the world; it is the price you can get by shipping cattle over to the United States. Anyone who wants to ship cattle there can do so. They say that ought to be the floor price on cattle. We agree with that and we have not attempted, except when we had foot-and-mouth disease in the country, to put a floor price under cattle.
Coming to hogs we find that 65 per cent of the basic price for grade B hogs is $19.99 and 85 per cent is $26.55, while the floor price for grade A is $23 at Toronto or Montreal. We are very close to the middle point, which is $23.07. Again the support price is much as they think it ought to be and as we think it ought to be.
Then we come to butter, upon which they have already expressed themselves, and I would not comment any further on these prices if it were not for filling out the table. We find that they calculate 65 per cent of parity to be 45-6 cents and 85 per cent of parity to be 59-7 cents. Our floor price is 58 cents. Canadian cheese works out to a range of from 23-1 to 33-3 cents, and I believe that today cheese is 33 cents if I read the market correctly this morning. This has been working along fairly well. We put up the 24-cent
Economic Position of Agriculture guarantee and the provincial government of Ontario puts up 6 cents, which makes it 30 cents.
There is a calculation for grade A eggs, Montreal, and a price of 41 cents is 65 per cent of parity and 85 per cent of parity is 53-6 cents. The support price we have established is 38 cents on December 1, for any eggs that are in store. Last year the price throughout the season was higher than this price at which we were stabilizing the price.
Now, I say that is the plan which has been worked out by the federation of agriculture, and I think it should be agreed that it is pretty well in line with what we have been doing by another method. There is one other matter that I think should be touched upon. A lot has been said about these income figures.
I am going to read a statement I got from the department as to what these figures mean:
The Farmer's Share of the National Income
There are no figures anywhere-
This is not my statement; this is a statement I got from the department.
There are no figures anywhere to show what the farmers' share of the national income actually is.
Why are there not?

That is a very good question. They tell me one of the reasons is that it would be a little costly. What I am going to ask you is, where did you get the figures you quoted? That is the purpose of reading this.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: From the bureau of statistics.

I continue :
The figures published by D.B.S. show:
1.	Income derived from sale of farm products;
2.	Income earned as wages and salaries, and
3.	Income from various types of production.
The income of farmers, like the income of many
other people, is derived from various sources. These are:
1.	The sale of farm products:
2.	Salaries and wages earned at non-farm work.
This is in brackets.
(In the United States it is estimated that more than one-third of the income of farmers comes from non-farm sources.)
3.	Income from investments. Many farmers have considerable sums invested in farm mortgages, in bonds, life insurance, and many other forms of investment. Income from these sources is not farm income in the normal sense but investment income.
4.	Income in kind and rent free housing. Farmers use their own food and live in their own houses.
Farm income figures published by D.B.S. attribute much lower values to these items than are actually paid by urban dwellers.
5.	The income of hired workers on farms is not listed as part of the farm income but rather as wage and salary income. It is estimated that there are approximately 80,000 hired men on Canadian farms. They probably earn $150 million a year. The hired men and their families, if any, are part of the farm population, but their income is classified properly with salaries and wages.

Economic Position of Agriculture
In the census returns any person living on an acre of land or more and deriving $250 or more from the sale of farm products is classified as a farmer. Farms of this sort probably make up one-quarter of the total number of farms listed in the census returns. The people concerned live on the farms, produce much of their own food but earn their cash income by other types of employment; many are persons who have retired on pension. The pensions are income but they are not listed as part of the farm income.
All of these facts prove beyond a doubt that the so-called farm income is not the equivalent of the income of farmers. Hence arguments based on the proposition that the farm income makes a smaller proportion of the national income than the farm population makes of the national population are fallacious.
And should be corrected.
Who prepared that statement?
It was prepared in the department.

speechtext: Which department?

The fact is that farms vary enormously in their earning power from area to area and from farm to farm.

The fact is that farms vary enormously in their earning power from area to area and from farm to farm. If my hon. friend will allow his mind to go back to the time when I last addressed this house, I gave the plan they used in the United States and they make out a net worth return which gives the figures. You do not have that here.

Gross income from the sale of farm products is determined by (a) the volume sold, and (b) price levels. In recent years income from the sale of milk and milk products in Canada has remained remarkably stable or has risen somewhat. On the other hand, income from the sale of wheat has declined heavily because of the low volume and low quality of the wheat produced in 1954 and because of a slower rate of sale than in the years between 1948 and 1953 when accumulated surpluses and heavy current production were both liquidated.
Meat prices reached abnormally high levels in 1950 and 1951 but declined sharply in the latter part of 1951. Beef prices have been relatively stable in the last three years, but pork prices have fluctuated fairly widely, mainly due to similar fluctuations in the United States pork markets. Prices of fruits and vegetables, especially apples and potatoes, have varied from very high to very low levels. Are my friends advocating that we should return to the conditions we had in 1951 and 1952 in order to give us that higher return?
There is only one reason why we had that high return in 1951 and 1952, and that is that we were at war in Korea. There is no other reason. There is only one reason for the increased cost of farm implements, and that reason is the preparations that we made for defence while we were at war in Korea and the preparations we are making for defence now. So, if my hon. friends are in the position where they are thinking in terms of how we are going to balance these things, then I would suggest to them that, in order to follow the plan they have been following in their speeches, they will have to depart entirely from the program they had before them when they came to this house about 20 years ago. As a matter of fact, I heard members on the floor of this house say they were particularly pleased that their sons had come to them and

said they would take no part. That is not the policy that is being talked of today.
If members on the other side of the house actually disagree with the policies of this government, which result in high expenditures in order to keep up defence, they ought to get up and say so, as they did before these policies were put into effect some years ago. This government has laid down a policy in connection with these matters. Of course, it is costly; it requires great taxation; it requires that farmers pay more taxes than they ever paid before across this country; and it requires, too, that costs of implements made out of steel, implements made out of aluminum, clothing made out of wool or any other fibre, all these are more costly in this country today because we find it necessary to carry on with those policies.
If my hon. friends are going to be honest with themselves and the voters in advocating their policies, they are going to come right out and say either that it should be done or it should not be done. I suggest to them that, if it should be done, there is not much possibility of changing the cost of some of the things that are made out of those materials. Those costs are going to stay up so long as it is necessary to carry on those policies. Neither this government nor any other government in a country so small as this in population can do very much about that, but we are hopeful that the policies of this government, the policies of the farmers in producing food for people throughout the world, and other policies will result in a condition of peace among the nations of the world that will make it possible for us not only to put down the prices of the things the farmer needs but make it possible for them to put them down.

In rising to take part in this debate on the amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply and on the subamendment, I do so with great pleasure. However, before commencing my remarks, I must pay my compliments to the Minister of Agriculture. As I mentioned in another speech, he is a wonderful man. He reminds me somewhat of the United States, of which we have had so much mention this afternoon. He reminds me somewhat of a great orator, shall I say, such as the late Senator Borah of the United States, or the late Huey Long.
We have been told this afternoon in a speech that took nearly two hours that the plight of agriculture in Canada is not too bad. With that impression, which the minister left with me, I must almost immediately take exception. I was very pleased that at the close of his talk the hon. member for Mackenzie got from the minister the statement that the farmers of Canada were perhaps entitled to a slightly larger share of the national income. With that premise before me, I propose to commence.
This amendment is one that should appeal to agriculture from Nova Scotia westward to British Columbia. It should appeal to the potato grower of Prince Edward Island; to the apple grower of Nova Scotia; to the potato grower of New Brunswick; to the dairy farmer of Quebec; to the stock man, the fruit producer and, shall I say, the tobacco raiser of Ontario; to the beekeeper of Manitoba; and now I come to Saskatchewan. I did have in mind to say the grain farmers of Saskatchewan but perhaps, as I followed the course of the minister's remarks so closely, I should say something, about the cement farmers of Saskatchewan as well, the stock raisers of

Economic Position of Agriculture Alberta, the fruit growers of British Columbia. This particular amendment appeals to all branches of agriculture. It is national in scope. It does not select any particular phase of the industry. It requests parity prices for agriculture generally throughout Canada. We are not any longer going to hear through the halls of this building, "We have heard enough about wheat; we have heard too much about wheat". Today we are pleading in the interests of agriculture throughout all of Canada.
To me this particular amendment is one that should transcend the realm of party politics. Apparently it did not do that. I feel that the plight of agriculture in Canada at the present time is something that should be beyond party political lines. History shows us, Mr. Speaker, what happens to great nations when the governments of those nations let agriculture go down. We have had a great deal of history this afternoon. We have been taken from 1930 right up to 1956. Let me go back a little bit prior to that. Let me go back to the good old Roman days. What happened to the Roman empire when they let their agricultural industry decay? It went down slowly and steadily to oblivion.

Maybe they had a Gardiner but they did not have a guardian to see that that did not happen. Again, to come back to modern times, may I point out that students who have studied the cause of the great depression in the United States in the thirties find now that one of the first danger signals which pointed to this ever-approaching depression in the United States was the sorry plight in which agriculture found itself in the United States during the twenties. Also coupled with this danger signal we find that they say that the ever-increasing instalment buying of the people of the United States was another danger signal. Mr. Speaker, I submit that we have those two danger signals right here in Canada today. I am only sorry that our present government is not prepared to pay more attention to these signals that we have with us.
I was very happy in January to notice that the leader of the great republic to the south of us, namely President Eisenhower, in his message on the state of the union assured the farmers of that country that federal administration was prepared to see that agriculture remained a stabilized industry in the United States. I should be only too happy if the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) would come before this house with a similar statement.
We have gone back to 1951 already this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. May I take you back just once more. I want to take you back to


December, 1951, and to the city of Saskatoon. I am quoting from a statement to be found in the Ottawa Journal. It is dated December 7, Saskatoon. The headline of this article runs in this way, "Howe reminds wheat farmer taxpayers raised $65 million". I will quote just a bit further from this article:
Mr. Howe told the delegates: "You have asked the people of Canada for help on many occasions and it is not so long ago that the taxpayers came through with $65 million"-the reference was to the final payment on the five-year wheat pool.
Just in that connection, Mr. Speaker, I wish to put on the record once again a statement which was made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) no later than yesterday. He had this to say, as reported at page 2034 of Hansard:
I have in my hand figures showing the losses that were suffered under the British wheat agreement by comparison with the world market price for class II wheat in the years 1946 to 1950, during which period the farmers lost $431,676,844. Then as the result of subsidizing the Canadian consumer at the same price at which we sold wheat to Britain instead of at the world market price, the farmers lost another $136,920,921. If you add those two figures together you get an over-all total of $568,597,765. If you subtract that from that figure $65 million which the government paid to the farmers on account of their losses, you have a net loss of approximately half a billion dollars.
Still in 1951 one of the leading spokesmen of this government reminded the farmers of the west that the taxpayers of Canada had come through with a measly $65 million. Then coming right up to January of this year the same right hon. gentleman, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), has this to say or it is reported that he had this to say: "Booming economy sees good year ahead". Every branch of industry in Canada, according to the statement, is booming. The statement was supposed to have originated from the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Every branch of industry in Canada is booming with the exception of one, and what is it?
Agricultural income, down in recent years, appears to have about reached a current bottom.
Mr. Speaker, I noticed with great interest that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had searched through the records for evidence to advance showing that the farmers of Canada were not in favour of parity prices. He must have been working about the same time as I was because this afternoon I wish to submit evidence to this house which I believe will support the pleas for parity prices. These pleas that I am going to bring in here this afternoon have been made by every farm organization throughout Canada. In starting on this discussion I might point out that in western Canada we have an active and aggressive farmers' organization which is rapidly growing eastward

across Canada. I am referring particularly to the interprovincial farm union council. This interprovincial farm union council has for years been submitting briefs to the federal government. I do not want to start at 1951 because it would take too much time and I have not an hour and forty minutes at my disposal at the present time. I want to point out that this is the submission made to the federal government on March 16, 1953. In dealing with livestock marketing they had this to say:
There is considerable evidence to indicate that our western livestock industry is lacking in required stability; this applies not only to cattle and hogs but also poultry and other livestock products.
That was a submission made to the federal government on March 16, 1953.
Again on page 5 of the same submission they have this to say:
We believe that as long as there are millions of people in the world who are underfed, as evidenced by reports of FAO, that every encouragement-even emphasis-ought to be placed on an all-out production program to bolster dwindling supplies of much needed foodstuffs. However, if as a result of such a program surpluses are built up, then provision should be made that such surpluses-be they long or short term-are not allowed to interfere with the prices on our home market.
At the same time, the interprovincial farm council pointed out this:
Farmers have often been penalized by even smali temporary surpluses, and the export price of their products have determined the price on the home market even in cases where only a small percentage of the total production was exported, and the largest share of it used for home consumption.
We realize, Mr. Speaker, as the minister pointed out this afternoon, that the vast percentage of livestock raised in Canada is consumed in Canada. We can see no reason for the general decline in the price of livestock during recent years.
Again in May of the same year a submission was made by the interprovincial farm union council to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization of this house. They had this to say. I think this is the keynote of their submissions throughout the years.
The prosperity of agriculture, like any other industry or individual, cannot be judged by any calculation based on gross receipts, but it is the farmers' net income or "take home pay" that really tells the story. While it is admitted that the gross income to the agricultural industry has been increasing, like all other major economic groups in Canada, the fact remains that the net income to agriculture has been decreasing, and. in spite of the higher than average production recently, we are concerned to find that the amount of agricultural improvement loans are, of necessity, rapidly increasing. The amount owing to finance corporations on purchases of various types, as well as the outstanding accounts to local merchants, are a further matter of deep concern, and we are somewhat fearful that the present prices and income to western agriculture, as our share
Economic Position of Agriculture of the national income, does not leave the farmers sufficient reserves to protect them from the natural production hazards to which the agricultural industry is annually subjected.
We believe that some definite steps must be taken by the government of Canada to raise the basic prices for agricultural commodities, and particularly that portion of our production sold on our domestic markets and consumed in Canada,_____
That was a submission made in May, 1953. Then again, the same brief deals with livestock marketing and says:
To those who have made a study of the present unsatisfactory situation of livestock marketing, the need for some new and definite program on a national or regional basis for establishing a plan of forward pricing in order to give the necessary stability to this most important branch of agriculture is becoming more and more evident.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in November, 1953, the same body in their submission to the government of Canada presented the following, dealing with livestock markets. They were not dealing with the price of wheat, the shortage of box cars or the weather, but with livestock markets.
The farm unions are very concerned with the lack of long range stability of our livestock markets. We fail to see any Justifiable reason why livestock prices, particularly beef cattle, should have been so drastically reduced to farmers.
Then, farther down:
"We note in this September's issue of 'Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada', issued by the federal Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, that our own Canadian people consumed 95 per cent of our total marketings of cattle and that only approximately 5 per cent was surplus for export during the first seven months of 1953."
Therefore, our own government publication provides conclusive proof that the so-called overproduction bogey, so often advanced by others as an excuse for lowering prices to farmers is a myth at this period.
Now, in February, 1954, the Canadian farm union council made another submission to the government and they said:
We believe the government's floor price system is inadequate for the producer;
Now, this has been brought out time and time again during the course of this session, with particular reference to the floor price on hogs. The matter of whether or not that floor price is being maintained across Canada is of great concern to the people of western Canada. I continue to quote:
-in many instances only the packers and processors have benefited by the government's support policy. A fundamental flaw in the present Agricultural Prices Support Act is the absence of a proper price formula for establishing floor prices.
What happens far too often is that the floor price becomes the maximum price paid for that particular type of goods. Farm machinery has been mentioned by the minister and he explained the reason for the price of farm machinery being so high. I cannot

Mr. Speaker, I am not a backbencher from

Economic Position of Agriculture western Canada but I am a backbencher from eastern Canada and I am interested in farm problems because my riding is half rural and half urban.
Much has been said today about the reduction in farm income. The right hon. minister at the last of his very worth-while review today said it was his opinion that in some cases farm income was down. In certain respects that definitely applies in my riding. In Grey county we produce, as farmers, cattle, pork, poultry, apples and dairy products. Dairy products, of course, remained on an even keel in 1955, thanks to the floor support plan of the government. Poultry and eggs were up a little bit. Cattle remained fairly steady but hogs and apples were away off. The reduction in the price of pork was very serious to a great many of the farmers in my riding because Grey county is one of the leading pork producing districts in Ontario.
The farmers in my constituency realize there is no easy solution to these problems. They realize that if a solution could come about by doing any of the things suggested by the C.C.F. group or by the resolution which was put on the order paper by the hon. member for Prince Albert, this government would have done it a long time ago. The farmers in my area recognize and appreciate the agricultural support policy of this government and the other farm policies that have been invoked by the present Minister of Agriculture.
The hon. member for Prince Albert in introducing his resolution stated that the farm policy of this government operated on a hit-or-miss basis. The farmers in my area do not feel that way. They appreciate particularly the floor support program. They recognize, for instance, that hogs were supported during the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease at 26 cents and cattle at 25 cents. Not only was the floor support beneficial, we all know the support prevented the collapse of the hog market at that time. The same obtains on eggs. Eggs dropped to 19 cents a dozen in 1949. The minister stepped in and supported them at 38 cents, which means about 32 cents to the producer, and since that time eggs have not fallen through the support except on one occasion last year and that was of brief duration and the minister quickly corrected it.
We all know that other products have been supported, such as cheese, milk, apples, butter and potatoes, to mention only a few.
At the present time the floor 'under hogs is 23 cents. We do not think it is enough but I would like to put on Hansard the fact that if

it were not for that floor support hogs would be selling at a much lower price than they are today. It goes without saying that we people who represent farm ridings will support any workable and practical measure that will raise the price of cattle and of hogs because it is in the interest of all of us. No matter what we interpret the word "parity" as meaning, we want the farmer to have his fair share of the national income.
I do not know what the hon. member for Prince Albert has in mind as a means of achieving this position of parity. He did not say very much about that; all he complained about was that prices were down. He did not give us any of his ideas as to how he was going to get the price of hogs or cattle to where he considers the prices would be at parity. He said only that we should have teeth in our hog floor legislation. Even if we have teeth in the legislation it does not put the price up to 26, 27.or 28 cents where we would all like to see it. That is the trouble with all the people who have been talking on the other side of the house. They say, "Let us have prices where they should be," but they do not give us any constructive ideas concerning how to do it.
If the hon. member for Prince Albert was thinking in terms of a higher floor he knows, of course, that many factors have to be taken into consideration. If we put up the price on hogs by means of a floor that contains an inducement to produce, I think we will all readily recognize that the farmer with two or three sows will soon have four or five, and the fellow living at the edge of town who has not gone into pigs will soon go into pigs. We found that out in 1952 when the floor was 26 cents. We did not think it was too high for hogs at all but we found that the government ended up with a great deal of pork. That floor support program in 1952 cost the government $35 million for hogs and $33 million for cattle but it was certainly money well spent in the national interest.
The United States has discovered, and the minister mentioned this, that if you have your floor support too high without any quotas or without a marketing scheme you soon have a surplus which will depress prices and will hurt the farmer in the long run. That is why Mr. Eisenhower in an election year, trying desperately to do something for the farmers did not, you will notice, come up with anything for the cattle producer or the hog producer because the surpluses in the United States are depressing prices.
In this country we are up against another problem. If we have our floor support high enough to attract United States cattle and hogs, after the duty and freight have been

paid, which do not amount to too much, our floor would be supporting the entire North American continent and we just cannot afford to do that.
I would like to mention an exception to the general rule. Hon. members will recall that a few weeks ago United States livestock was coming into Canada because prices there for the first time were lower than ours. I received representations to the effect that we should close the border. This, of course, would be an extremely narrow and short-term policy. As the minister said today, the United States has always been our floor for cattle. There are 160 million people there and it is a great potential market for our farmers.

My hog producer is very much interested in the supreme court reference mentioned today by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). While some of my farmers are still individualists, more and more they are coming to believe that they must have a marketing scheme, preferably one run by themselves through a marketing board, in order to have orderly marketing and establish the prices which they should get on the market. I must say that I personally am coming more and more to that line of thinking.
I happen to be in the apple business and with a bumper crop this year we had no control over the marketing of apples. Without any government assistance at all-we are not asking for that-without any floor support if we had had a marketing agency so that we would have had some over-all control over the marketing of our apples we would have been much better off this year.
My hog producers feel the same way. I was glad to hear the minister say that there is to be a conference with the provincial ministers of agriculture to discuss marketing legislation. I think that is a step in the right direction. Whether we believe in quotas or just selling through a central agency under a free enterprise system, I think there should be marketing schemes and marketing boards.

If the minister does not mind, I should like to urge him, if the decision of the supreme court is to the effect that the marketing legislation of the Ontario government is ultra vires and further authority is needed, to see that legislation is ready to be passed at this session. That is one thing we can do to help the farmer to set up machinery so that he can help himself.
My riding is very important from an apple producing point of view. The famous Beaver valley and Georgian bay apples are grown in my district. There are very important orchards too in the Meaford area. I see the hon. member for Durham (Mr. James) is looking at me, and I am ready to admit that perhaps there are some McIntosh apples down there although I have never heard of them too often.
As I have said, we had a bumper crop in the Georgian bay district this year. I am not


appealing to the government for any help and I am not even going to offer any constructive suggestions. The only thing I would like to say is that we have had a very poor year. I have heard some hon. members from Nova Scotia and British Columbia complaining, and I just want to assure the house that the Georgian bay grower did not make any money this year either. With our large crop we had high costs for containers, spraying materials, labour and fertilizers. In the end the small grower, if not the large grower, lost money. Instead of the price of apples being $2.50 or $2.75 per bushel, apples were selling at around $1 per bushel and some apples were not even picked.
The Ontario growers this year went on record as being against the idea of a subsidy and perhaps I should explain that. They do not think that the government should grant subsidies year after year to encourage the growing of varieties of apples where it is not economical to grow them. They emphatically oppose the granting of subsidies which help the growers of another province to compete in their traditional markets in Ontario. I remember that four or five years ago this government did one of the few things it has ever done wrong: a subsidy was granted to the apple growers of another province and the following week these growers took the back page of the Star Weekly and did considerable harm in our traditional Ontario-Toronto market. Using your own money to ruin your own market is certainly rubbing it in.
I hope the minister will continue the generous grants which have been made under the Cold Storage Act. We found this year that there was a scarcity of cold storage in Ontario and many McIntosh apples were put on the market because of lack of storage. That is another way in which this government is helping the farmer and can continue to help him.
Turning from apples, I should like to speak briefly about butter. The price of butterfat and cream was and is one of the bright spots in the farm picture in my riding. I never hear complaints about the price of butterfat. Most farmers are high in their praise of our butter policy. Our butter policy has been stated many times as being a means whereby the government purchases butter during the heavy butter producing months and feeds it back to the consumer during the winter months, thus stabilizing the price and helping both the consumer and the farmer. The farmer is able to get the same or higher price all the year round, and by putting purchasing power in the hands of the farmer we are helping the whole economy.

I urge the government to maintain this support price of 58 cents under butter. Much has been said about the importance of the dairy industry and I do not think I need to elaborate on that. In my riding the cream cheque is spent on Saturday night or during the week end by the farmer and his wife and is quickly distributed throughout the economy to the benefit of all. Last year the cream producers of Grey county were paid close to $3 million and it will be appreciated what that meant to a riding such as mine.
I am not afraid that the government will abandon the floor price under butter, but I am a little nervous that they may drop it 2 or 3 cents. Some hon. members seem to believe that more butter would be sold and consumed if the price were dropped 2 or 3 cents, but I do not hold that view at all. By thus reducing the purchasing power of the farmer you would be working to the detriment of the whole economy. We have margarine eaters and we have butter eaters and the spread in price between the two is too great to induce some margarine eaters to eat butter just because the price has been dropped 3 or 4 cents.
When introducing this resolution the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was critical of the sales which have been made to iron curtain countries. I think too the hon. member who spoke last referred rather disparagingly of this policy. They ask: Why give bargains to communist countries? I suppose that is a pretty popular thing to say, but I submit that the government policy is the correct one. My farmers certainly think it is the correct one.
If the hon. member for Prince Albert considers we can take 15 million or 20 million pounds of butter surplus and dispose of that in a special sale I would like to ask him how he expects to get around the administrative problem. There are thousands of retail and wholesale outlets and how could you make sure that the bargain of 20 or 25 cents was being passed on to the consumer. A sale of 15 million pounds would last only two weeks and would mean a saving of only 25 cents to each person in Canada. I do not think you could do it, but even if you could there would be the more serious objection that you would be undermining the permanent price of butter. We might get away with one fire sale at 40 cents and go back to 65 cents, but you could not do it more than once or twice. The housewives just would not buy butter for 65 cents after getting it at 40 cents. The result would be that sooner or later you would be bringing down the price of butter, and the 67509-133J	; |
Economic Position of Agriculture price would be determined for the 317 million pounds we produce in Canada by that small surplus of 15 million pounds.
I have listened very carefully to the members of the opposition on this butter question and I cannot for the life of me figure out what they advocate. They seem to be in favour of this 58 cents support, although they do not underline its importance to the farmer. They do not say what they are in favour of. Some members opposite apparently are in favour of the two price plan and one of the leading associations interested in the dairy industry in Canada is also in favour of this two-price scheme. Under that scheme, of course, butter would be allowed to find its own level, say 40 cents, and the government would continue to support the producer at 58 cents per pound, paying to the producer 18 cents per pound. You can see how much that would cost by multiplying 18 or 20 cents by 317 million. It would cost $60 million a year, unless of course you had a quota system. That was the plan that was advocated by Mr. Brennan in the United States, but the republicans and democrats over there found that that just would not work, because the cost was prohibitive.
You may say, "Let us have a quota." If you are going to have a quota, you must have a marketing board, and that is a different story altogether. But I do not think we should disturb our butter policy, which is the bright spot in my riding. My farmers say to me, "If you do not say anything else in this session, get up and praise the minister for the 58 cents support, because it is essential to keep it."
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) made a very worth-while contribution in the throne speech debate and he quoted some figures that showed that the gap between production and consumption, was 17 million pounds this year. He was worried that that gap might increase, although his figures do not bear that out. In 1953, for instance, the gap was 17 million pounds. In 1954 it was 20 million; and in 1955 it was estimated at 17 million pounds. The president of the Canadian federation of agriculture does not agree that the gap is going to widen; he thinks it is going to close. It is difficult to say what will happen. There are some people who think we are going to be short of butter in three years. The gap might well be closed in one year with the wrong weather. It might be closed on account of our growing population. It is obvious that there are many factors, and it is difficult for anybody to say right now what the situation is going to be with regard to butter two or three years from now. That is all the more reason why we should keep to the present policy.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment that we are considering and the subamendment are as follows. The amendment moved by the hon. member far Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) reads:
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship".
Then the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) moved his subamendment which reads:
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding thereafter the following words:
"in such a manner as to provide for a fair share of the national income for agriculture".
The only reason that I read the amendment and the subamendment is that I cannot see that the subamendment adds anything to the amendment. I would think that the subamendment is redundant, Mr. Speaker. I do not expect you to rule on that point. But if parity means equality, then if there were parity prices as set out in the amendment it would naturally flow from that "in such manner as to provide for a fair share of the national income for agriculture". If you accept that parity means fair, then certainly the subamendment does not add anything to the amendment. There are of course two ideas about the word "parity". To me parity means par, something that is equal. But apparently there is another more technical meaning attached to the word "parity". The hon. member for Assiniboia sets out clearly what he and his party think the word "parity"

means. As reported at page 2026 of Hansard, the hon. member for Assiniboia said:
I want to point out to hon. members of this house that the concept of parity prices is that the government shall so regulate the prices of farm products as to give to agriculture an income which bears a very direct relationship to the income of other groups in our economy.
Then he goes on to chide the Conservative party for getting away from their free enterprise thinking. That kind of parity I do not believe in. I think it has been shown many times that it would be impossible for this government to set floor prices which would contain an inducement to produce. As I said before the dinner recess, our experience during the foot and mouth disease epidemic, when we literally got up to our necks in hogs because the floor price of 26 cents contained an element of profit, I think, was a lesson to all of us. Let us take, for example, potatoes. I would ask the hon. member for Assiniboia whether, if there were a fixed parity price for potatoes, which contained a profit element would not half of the whole province of Ontario be planted out in potatoes. I know that my county would be. I do not think you can work that conception of parity unless you have marketing boards and quotas. You must have control over production. If the resolution means that kind of parity, I am against it. But if it means parity prices, with the intent that the farmer shall get his fair share of the national income, I think everybody in the house is in favour of it.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the debates which have taken place in the house during this session on agricultural problems. I have not taken part in those particular debates, but I believe there are two factors which might qualify me for doing so and which would warrant my participation in debates on agriculture. One is the fact that I was raised on a farm, a farm where they grew a lot of that wheat we have been hearing about, and the other is that I represent a predominantly agricultural area in British Columbia.
I have been endeavouring to fit into the general framework of our discussion this serious problem to which I :hould like to call attention at this time. It has to do with the serious situation which exists in British Columbia because of the exceptionally severe frosts which struck the province during November last year. Perhaps I should say that we are not used to having severe frosts in British Columbia at any time, and certainly last year was the exception. Not only did it come with great intensity, it came at an early period in the season when no one was expecting it or was prepared for it. The result was that the agricultural producers in my area and in other areas as well suffered very severe losses.
I should like to call attention to this situation tonight. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) intends to make some remarks in this connection. I know that his remarks will be perhaps complementary to

mine and will carry forward some of the statements which I shall make at this time.
The problem which faces us is a serious one. Since these frosts occurred a number of briefs have been drawn up by various interested parties and groups of individuals for presentation to different organizations and governmental authorities. I have one here dealing with frost injury to nursery stock which was prepared by the Canadian association of nurserymen, British Columbia division, in co-operation with the Vancouver island association of nurserymen. It was compiled at the request of nurserymen operating in British Columbia and is the result of a fairly complete survey representing approximately 90 per cent of the nursery injury. It indicates the extent of the frost damage throughout the province and brings to the attention of governmental authorities the problem which the producers are facing. It asks also for financial assistance in one form or another. I should like to place on the record one paragraph from this particular brief to be found on page 2 which reads:
The resulting losses sustained by nurseries are of such a serious nature that the future of the industry is seriously threatened.
Some nurseries have lost up to 85 per cent of their total production not only for this year but also to their young stock coming along for future years. For example, cherry trees are among the most seriously damaged. The growers have lost all their one year trees which were ready for sale during fall 1955, spring 1956. They have lost a large proportion of the young stock coming along for 1956-57. It will therefore be 1957-58 before a normal crop will again be available and this will be contingent upon the nurserymen being able to finance through this period from 1955 to 1958 when returns from production of this crop should again commence coming in.
This same situation applies to peaches, apricots and some apple varieties although the damage is not as extensive as for cherries.
The estimated losses to nursery stock at wholesale prices for the different regions are as follows:
Vancouver island	 $ 75,455.70
Lower mainland	 210,159.65
Interior	 73,757.00
Total	 $359,372.35
We must realize that not only have severe losses been suffered by those engaged in this industry; there will be repercussions in various other fields as well. Employment may be threatened, as already some of the grower nurseries have laid off approximately 80 per cent of their field staff. As I intimated at the beginning of my remarks, this brief states that as a result of the frost losses this industry is in grave danger of extinction. Part of the last paragraph of the brief reads:
Assistance of a very concrete nature is urgently needed and this submission is made in the hope

that help will be forthcoming and that it will be of a nature appropriate to the gravity of the situation.
That has to do only with the production of nursery stock,	one	particular	phase of	theindustry in British	Columbia.	I should	like
to call attention as well to the losses suffered by the berry growers of British Columbia, especially the strawberry growers who have suffered a crippling blow. The bureau of statistics gives the following farm value of strawberry production in different years:
1952		 $2,163,000
1953		 2,716,000
1954		 2,531,000
Raspberry growers also suffered seriously from the frost, and in the case of this group the production values are as follows:
1952		 $1,256,000

We can see by this that this is an industry that is vital to the economy of British Columbia and certainly, speaking for my own riding of Fraser Valley, it is of tremendous importance to us in that section. The estimated loss, as far as the strawberry stock is concerned, is just about 100 per cent. The estimated loss for raspberries for the coming year would be 80 per cent, and possibly that loss would be reduced a little each year as they get back into production.
We can see that this is a very serious problem which our producers are facing at this time. A table has been drawn up. I am not going to take time to read it but, unless assistance is forthcoming, the total estimated losses are as follows: for 1955, $2,214,070; for 1956, $7,086,500. The estimated loss between 1955 and 1960 is $17,244,570.
Following the disaster last fall, meetings were held in the various sections of the Fraser valley to consider what steps should be taken and what approach should be made to the governments in their quest for assistance under these difficult circumstances. It was decided at some of these meetings to make an appeal to the provincial government of British Columbia, and that was done.
Following the appeal to the provincial government, they decided to carry the matter further by an appeal to the federal government for some type of assistance. On February 9 I asked the Minister of Agriculture in this house whether he had received a request from the representatives of the berry growing industry for a meeting, and the reply I received at that time was that the Minister of Agriculture had received communications in this respect from the representatives of the berry growers and he had also received a communication from the provincial government.

The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in their annual presentation to the Prime Minister of Canada and members of the cabinet, Ottawa, February 14, 1956, had this to say in paragraph 3 on page 13:
To establish a policy for providing emergency or disaster credit on an interest-free basis where the nature and extent of a farmer's loss justifies the granting of such credit. It should be noted in this connection that the growing demand for some disaster loan legislation was reflected again this year, in resolutions coming before the federation's annual convention. Because of the fact that there is no existing credit legislation to cover emergency situations of this kind, it is a matter of the most immediate and vital importance that such legislation be provided. The extensive losses due to frost suffered by strawberry and other fruit, vegetable and flower growers in B.C. is a case in point, and the damage was sufficiently severe that U.S. coastal states, struck by the same frosts, were declared emergency disaster areas by the United States government.
I want to make it clear that these farmers, like the farmers in other areas, are not asking for handouts. I just want to refer to the brief of a group of Fraser valley small fruit farmers presented to the minister of agriculture of the province of British Columbia

When a large group of fanners are in financial straits, all businesses in their communities suffer likewise but if financial aid is forthcoming to the farmer, he, and his community, can carry on at a nearer to normal level. Although suffering great losses, the berry growers at the aforementioned meetings stated they did not wish to receive grants in the form of financial aid but rather, as a free enterprise industry, they stand on their own feet and meet this crisis in the normal manner of securing a loan to rehabilitate themselves.
Let me therefore state again that they are not asking for just a handout but that they are asking that credit facilities be placed at their disposal whereby they can again get into business and carry on with the normal processes of agriculture. Just to make this point clear and to emphasize what their request really is,. It is with the above serious situation in mind,-
They are referring to the losses and also to the cost of rehabilitating the industry:
-we formally request the government of the Dominion of Canada to take steps to prepare the necessary legislation which will make immediately available long term low interest loans and/or government backed bank loans to those sections of the agricultural industry who require assistance.
Mr. Speaker, I have given some consideration to various measures, wondering whether it would be possible to fit this objective in within the framework of any of the existing legislation such as the farm loan act or the farm improvement act, but it seems as though some amendment will be necessary in order to accomplish that objective. I may be wrong in my deduction but it would appear to me that that would be the case. Just to mention some of the obstacles in the way of coverage through the farm loan act, there is the matter of the first mortgage; and I might say that this would constitute an extremely serious handicap or obstacle because of the fact that there are a number of the farms that already are mortgaged. Again, the assessed value of farms under this particular measure are still too low to bring the necessary help to these farmers. Certainly the interest rates are far too high. That matter has been mentioned in other connections as well. Then there is the matter of the time required to appraise all the farms that would be affected in these particular circumstances. I notice that under the regulations the assessments would be made between May 1 and December 1 and,

Nevertheless, the delay that would be occasioned by assessing all these individual farms would carry the matter far beyond the time when assistance would bring the desired results.
As we look at the particular act I have mentioned, it seems as though its provisions would not be sufficient to bring the assistance that is needed. It may be possible, I am not sure, that under the Farm Improvement Loans Act some assistance may be given. But again, I have been unable to see just where these conditions would fit in under the regulations made under that particular measure.
Coming back, Mr. Speaker, to the meeting of the delegation with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) I may say they were under the impression-perhaps the minister will correct me if I am wrong or if they are wrong-that the minister said that so far no proposals had been forthcoming from the provincial government.
I did not say that, Mr. Speaker, because I had a telegram and a letter from them on my desk.

I might inform the minister I have followed his political activities even before the days when he became the federal Minister of Agriculture. We in the C.C.F. group are ever willing to support any section of the Canadian population that is adversely affected by conditions beyond their control. We are on the record on innumerable occasions asking the government to help our people who are adversely affected. Only the other day I indicated that I was in full accord in the main with the activities of the fisheries prices support board. We have been consistent supporters of the Unemployment Insurance Act, under which workers who lose their source of income through no fault of their own are assured of at least a minimum income. In this instance several thousand farmers have suffered terrific losses. I am not going to bother the house with any figures. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has ably placed them on the record. However, when you have a group of farmers whose plants have been wiped out to the extent of 75 per cent to 80 per cent, who have no hope of income in 1956, and very little hope of any income in 1957, I feel the subject should not become a matter of political expediency, as I am afraid this may well have become.
I noted the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to how these farmers might possibly be helped. I do not need to comment upon that. I am sure the minister is resourceful enough to find ways and means of using the existing legislation, or asking the house to amend existing legislation, so that the help that is asked for might be forthcoming.
I should like to remind the government that if this catastrophe had hit almost any other section of the Canadian economy the people would have been running to Ottawa asking for a handout. I should like to commend the berry growers on their modest appeal. On page 4 of the brief that they prepared initially for presentation, as is proper, to their own minister of agriculture in British Columbia, they said:
They did not wish to receive grants in the form of financial aid.
Farther on they said:
They stand on their own feet and wish to meet this crisis in the normal manner of securing a loan to rehabilitate themselves.
I would have thought that an appeal of such a nature might find some measure of response.
I notice in the press that the attitude of the government seems to be that this is something that is not beyond the abilities of the government of British Columbia to deal with. I agree it is not beyond the abilities of the government of British Columbia adequately to meet the situation. However, Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why the government of British Columbia should be asked to

In many other instances we have had the federal government helping out where the provincial government was also able by itself to take care of the situation. I am thinking of the flash flood that occurred in the city of Toronto at the time of "Hurricane Hazel". Nobody can tell me that the government of Ontario was so hard up that it would have been unable to meet the situation. However, the federal government- and I am pleased to note this-did not hesitate to share a part of the load at that time. I cannot blame the government of British Columbia for asking the federal government to share the risk that might be involved in meeting these very modest demands of the berry farmers on a fifty-fifty basis.
If I have any complaint at all about the government of British Columbia in this matter it is that it introduced a bill in the British Columbia legislature and obtained the consent of that legislature under which the government is authorized to spend up to a certain amount of money to guarantee loans to those farmers if the federal government will share the risk with them. I feel that the condition which they attached to their bill completely ties their hands so that in the event that Ottawa turns them down-and I hope Ottawa will not turn them down in the long run-the British Columbia government will be unable to render the help that these farmers so badly need.
I feel the British Columbia government made a mistake. They should have left the door wide open so that if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) continues to think this is a relatively unimportant problem, unworthy of his attention, the government of British Columbia would be able to act on its own and look after the situation.
I know the favourite reply that we often get from the government on difficulties of this kind. It is that if people cannot make their living in this way they should turn to something else.
Again I should like to refer to the brief- I will not read it-which very adequately points out why these berry farmers are unable to follow the advice that is so glibly given to them to start growing vegetables or potatoes. They point out that they are unable to render effective competition to the mass produced vegetables from other more favourable areas of the province and south of the border. The fact that there may be no berry crop in British Columbia will be felt not only in that province but by the housewives of Alberta, Saskatchewan and the western part of Manitoba.
