"Fraser valley strawberry growers alone have lost 16,000,000 plants", he claimed.
"That alone is a disaster. It means they can produce no crop this year even if the plants are replaced."
The Department of Agriculture operates an experimental farm at Agassiz and undoubtedly the minister has been advised by the officials of that farm, who are most efficient in their way, that their nursery stock is gone, that they have no berry plants which might be supplied to the lower Fraser valley. If we are going to get plants it is necessary that enabling legislation be passed now or some form of assistance be made available to these farmers. This should be done now, not later in the year, because this is the time when farmers must set out new plants, otherwise they will lose another full year. This article goes on:
The position of the B.C. industries is worsened "because competitors in Washington and Oregon are to get federal aid,'' said another man.
"Those states, which also suffered in the frost, were declared to be disaster areas. So their growers' losses are being made good. We shall face their competition at a time when we can't possibly meet it unless we get help."
These particular farmers are not asking for financial help in the form of a grant; they are not asking for $30 million in the form of storage facilities or anything like that; all they want is what this government has been trying to press upon the farmers of the prairie provinces, that is, an opportunity to borrow. The government suggested that the prairie farmers be granted loans instead

Agriculture-Frost Damage in B.C. of advances, but these people do not want advances. All they want is the opportunity to borrow, and I submit that they have a just claim.
My grievance is that no means are made available whereby these people who are distressed may be able to stay in business. With this in mind, on January 30 I placed on the order paper a motion reading as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of setting up a committee composed of federal, provincial and municipal authorities or their representatives for the purpose of studying the problems of and determining what constitutes a disaster area in Canada.
I do not intend to debate that particular resolution at this time. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned earlier, it was considered desirable to give the people who suffered from "Hurricane Hazel" some assistance, and I submit that the same considerations should apply here. Only 3 per cent of the land of British Columbia is arable and most of the farmers of the province live in this particular area on 3,500 small farms. Those farmers are in dire need.
It is just twelve minutes to ten o'clock and I have only two short items that I wish to place before the minister in respect to this matter. The first is in the form of a brief, a copy of which I am satisfied the minister has. This reads in part:
It is with the above serious situation in mind, we formally request the government of the dominion of Canada to take steps to prepare the necessary legislation which will make immediately available long-term low interest loans and/or government backed bank loans to those sections of the agricultural industry who require assistance.
We hear a great deal about the federation of agriculture and the requests that it has made to the minister and the government. Reference has been made to some of those requests at an earlier date. The February 1956 issue of Country Life in British Columbia, a British Columbia publication, had this to say:
To meet disastrous situations a special type of federal government credit agency should be formed to be known as the agricultural emergency loan administration.
I do not intend to read any more of that because I am satisfied the minister is fairly familiar with it because he has been listening to the debates in this house. I feel quite sure that it would not be necessary to pass a completely new act as other means must be available or the Farm Improvement Loans Act could be amended in order that money could be put into the hands of these farmers so that they could put in their berry plants. I should like to have the minister comment upon the legislation the British Columbia


government has passed in respect to making loans available to these farmers.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the hon.
members who spoke a few minutes ago made the suggestion that we should do the same for farmers everywhere as we do for the wheat farmers, that we should give them the same consideration. This particular matter has to do with the obtaining of plants to be planted at the right time of the year for those who have had plants destroyed by frost.
We have had similar situations on previous occasions on the prairies and in other parts of Canada and they have always been looked after by the provincial governments. Someone said something about politics in connection with this, but it has not made any difference what political party was in power in the particular province. As I say, matters of this kind have been looked after by the provinces and provincial legislation has taken care of them.
For example, during the years when they had no crops on the prairie provinces and it was difficult to obtain seed, provision for obtaining that seed was made by the provincial governments at a cost of millions of dollars.
Who paid for it?

Someone asks, "Who paid
for it?" Members from Saskatchewan who are here ought to know who paid for it because it was partly on that issue that they won the province. The provincial governments paid the bill right through.
The matter of dealing with people in British Columbia will be handled just the same as it is anywhere else in Canada. All that was suggested to them was that this was a matter in connection with which the provincial government should take action. Even the delegation which was here understood that. The first letter that I had from the delegation was to the effect that they had seen the provincial government and they did not think that government was going to assume their responsibilities and therefore they came to us. When they got here I discussed the matter with them as I would discuss any matter with anyone who came here. I told them that the matter would be taken up with the treasury and others and I would give them an answer the following day. As I stated a few moments ago, I found that the letter which it was intended should go forward to them before had not left the office. I sent it to the hotel, and they obtained it, I presume, either that night or the following morning. I am not sure they actually came

back, but if they did they were only there for a very short time. But the suggestion was that they should discuss the matter further with the province, and we expected that we would probably hear more about it. So far as I know, we have not heard any more about it, and I assume somebody out there is dealing with the problem.
It is purely a provincial matter and always has been. The federal government never does say in connection with any matter brought in from the provinces that we will not even consider it. We listen to what they have to say, and, where it is a matter that should be looked after provincially, we simply say that, and sometimes that is the last we hear of it. At other times the province takes action and still asks us to help pay for it. In this particular case, as the hon. member has just said, it is a matter of guaranteeing loans of a certain kind in order to be able to buy plants. It is much the same in principle as the loans that were made to farmers to permit them to buy seed in other parts of the country. They eventually pay off these loans in some way or other.
I do not know that there is anything more I can say about it. I do not know whether or not we shall hear any more about it. If we do, we shall give whatever consideration we can to it and give advice along the same lines as in other parts of Canada. We are not going to make an exception of the case. We do not think this is something that is so costly or so difficult to arrange that the province is not able to do it. Knowing, as we do, it is a responsibility of the provinces, we think they should take action.

In the remaining few minutes I should like to deal very briefly with a problem that has become increasingly important in northern New Brunswick. It has to do with unemployment insurance.
The information I have gathered in the survey I have made across the northern part of New Brunswick in regard to unemployment insurance comes from employees and officials employed by the unemployment insurance commission itself. One of the gravest problems with which we have to deal is the fact that we do not have reciprocity in regard to unemployment insurance with the state of Maine.
The state of Maine is one of two states in all the United States of America that does not have unemployment insurance reciprocity with Canada. At the moment 1,800 men from the county of Madawaska and 6,000 men from all over Canada have been employed in Maine
Unemployment Insurance and are being denied unemployment insurance merely because this government has not taken steps to enter into reciprocity agreements with the state of Maine or, if it has entered into negotiations with the state of Maine, they have not been successful in getting that state to accept reciprocity with Canada. Our people who work there have to pay unemployment insurance; yet when they come back home they cannot collect unemployment insurance benefits.
Another very great problem, which I think has been brought up by several members on the other side of the house recently, had to do with the directives of the unemployment insurance commission in forcing men to go many hundreds of miles away from their homes to work under conditions that prohibit them from earning enough money to live, let alone enabling them to buy their tickets back home. Four hundred or five hundred people from the county of Restigouche were requested to go to La Tuque to cut pulpwood. Some did go, but were unable to earn enough money to buy their tickets back home. Some of them suffered many hardships, having to live in camps where they were improperly treated and the food was insufficient.
As I think has been brought up by several Liberal members recently, this dictatorship in the unemployment insurance commission must be forced to cease immediately. We cannot continue to force our people to accept employment many hundreds of miles away from their homes under conditions that prevent them from earning a living.
Another matter I wish to bring out this evening is this. Until two years ago, people cutting pulpwood on farms, that is, cutting pulpwood for farmers on farmers' lots, were able to get unemployment insurance. Two years ago this was abolished. I do not know why, but one thing is very certain. There was some suggestion at the time that abuses had crept in. I ask, are we going to prohibit driving on our highways because the odd man exceeds the speed limit? Are we going to abolish credit because the odd man does not pay his bills? Are we going to prohibit one class of people from unemployment insurance because possibly a few abuses have occurred? I am not denying those abuses, but I am saying that they in themselves, however true, are not sufficient to deny these people unemployment insurance benefits as a group.
Another point I wish to bring out in the next few minutes that remain to me is this. When I asked the Minister of Labour some weeks ago questions regarding unemployment insurance, the information that I had and on which my question was based came from officials and employees in the unemployment

They were bombarded with complaints and questions because of the tie-up and delays that were occurring in the unemployment insurance office in Moncton. This was very true. The minister answered my question three weeks after I asked him. There is no question but that in that time action had been taken to remove the causes of delay.
If the minister had taken time to inquire, he would have found out also that the R.C.M.P. had been sent to the Campbellton office to inquire and investigate and be on hand when a disturbance there threatened. These items may not appear to you, Mr. Speaker, to warrant the special few remarks that I am making here tonight, but I say that with all the approximately 6,000 people on unemployment insurance in northern New Brunswick, mostly in my riding, there are another 4,000 or 5,000 people in my riding who should be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits and who are not receiving them.
